During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), he said the TPLF violated the Pretoria Agreement signed in October 2022. The PM recalled that the key elements of the Pretoria Agreement included cessation of hostilities, restoration of all services, disarmament, return of displaced people, and recognition of the constitutional order. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The federal government had fulfilled everything that was possible and expected of it, he added. On the contrary, the TPLF had been purchasing and soliciting weapons as well as openly recruiting young people instead of implementing the agreement to disarm combatants. Above all, PM Abiy pointed out that after the agreement, the TPLF used displaced persons as hostages to prevent them from returning to their homes. Additionally, it engaged in destroying and closing down infrastructure--including airlines, banking, and telecommunications--that had been restored by the Federal Government to deliver services. Despite the group's misdeeds, the PM stated that the government had forewarned that war was not worthwhile and that peace was preferable. However, the TPLF disregarded the advice and collaborated with various forces, and violated the Pretoria Agreement by initiating an unnecessary war. Immense damage has been inflicted on the public as a result of the war instigated by the TPLF, he noted. War is bad and yields no benefit, the Premier further noted, adding that a war fought for the interests of foreign forces is even worse. The psychological damage is not to be taken lightly and damage has also been inflicted on development and the economy. PM Abiy stressed that young people carrying Kalashnikovs should therefore return to work and participate in the development and rehabilitation of Tigray. Noting that many young people were forcibly recruited, he advised those who have not yet returned to return to normal life. He stated that the leaders of the TPLF have been declaring war for 50 years without dying or being wounded themselves; instead they sent their children and families abroad and to Addis Ababa where they are engaged in business and construction. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Honors Kenya's Heroes, Highlights Shared Legacy of Unity - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Honors Kenya's Heroes, Highlights Shared Legacy of Unity 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has paid tribute to Kenya's freedom fighters and national heroes during the Mashujaa Day celebrations in Eldoret, Kenya. The Premier highlighted the shared legacy of courage, unity, and sacrifice between the two countries. In a social media post, the Prime Minister said: "I delivered remarks paying tribute to the heroes who fought for freedom and those who made the ultimate sacrifices to safeguard their nation. I honour their courage and legacy!" PM Abiy noted that Kenya's history of courage and sacrifice resonates deeply with Ethiopia's own story of Adwa, where Ethiopians from every corner of the country united to defend their homeland. These shared histories remind us that freedom was never given but won through courage, unity, and sacrifice, the Prime Minister added. "As our histories are intertwined, so too must our futures be. Through the spirit of Medemer, Ethiopia and Kenya must continue building on our existing cooperation in clean energy, connectivity, telecommunications, and trade to create greater opportunities and shared prosperity for our people," he said. The two countries also cooperate in regional security, cross-border infrastructure, trade, telecommunications, and electricity interconnections, supporting economic integration and development across the Horn of Africa, it was learned. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Calls for Data-Driven Policymaking to Accelerate Africa's Progress
ethiopia.content: Africa: Ethiopia Calls for Data-Driven Policymaking to Accelerate Africa's Progress - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Ethiopia Calls for Data-Driven Policymaking to Accelerate Africa's Progress 21 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia has reformed its statistical legislation and established an independent statistical service to strengthen the production and coordination of official data, President Taye Atske Selassie said. Taye underscored the importance of reliable statistics in driving evidence-based development in Africa. Addressing the opening of the 10th Session of the Statistical Commission for Africa and the 12th Meeting of the Regional Committee of the United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management for Africa in Addis Ababa, the President said Ethiopia's development planning is anchored in measurable targets and reliable data. He emphasized that development cannot be effectively planned, sustained, or scaled up without accurate measurement, noting that official statistics are essential for shaping development strategies, tracking progress, and strengthening accountability. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The President also highlighted Ethiopia's reforms in the financial and digital sectors, including the National Digital Payment Strategy, financial sector liberalization, interoperable payment infrastructure, and the national digital identification program, Fayda. He said Fayda enables secure electronic verification and expands access to banking, mobile money, telecommunications, and other essential public services, demonstrating how digital infrastructure can improve service delivery and financial inclusion. According to the President, mobile money and mobile banking accounts in Ethiopia reached 257 million and processed more than 24 trillion birr in transactions during the first nine months of 2026, reflecting the expansion of the country's financial and digital systems. Drawing lessons from these reforms, he stressed that statistics must serve as practical tools for sustainable development and be communicated clearly and accessibly to policymakers and citizens, rather than being treated as an end in themselves. He also called for statistical institutions to integrate and safeguard diverse data sources without compromising statistical integrity, emphasizing that innovation must reinforce data quality, institutional independence, and public trust. The President urged African governments to protect the professional independence of official statistics, strengthen legal and institutional frameworks, invest in national statistical systems, and ground policy decisions in scientific evidence. He cautioned that poor-quality data undermines evidence-based policymaking, impedes development, and weakens accountability. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is advocating for data-driven policymaking to enhance development across Africa, as emphasized by President Taye Atske Selassie during the 10th Session of the Statistical Commission for Africa. The country has reformed its statistical legislation and established an independent statistical service to improve the production and coordination of official data. President Taye highlighted the necessity of reliable statistics for effective development planning and accountability. He also discussed Ethiopia's advancements in financial and digital sectors, including the National Digital Payment Strategy and the Fayda digital identification program, which have significantly expanded access to essential services. The President urged African governments to protect the independence of statistical institutions and invest in national statistical systems, stressing that poor-quality data hinders evidence-based policymaking. The joint meetings aim to strengthen data systems and improve monitoring of development progress across the continent.

somalia.content: Ethiopia, Kenya and the Growing Complexity of Somalia’s Security Crisis – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 Ethiopia, Kenya and the Growing Complexity of Somalia’s Security Crisis 0 Comments Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s visit to Kenya on October 20 came at a time when Ethiopia’s relations with its neighbours are increasingly shaped by competing security concerns and shifting regional alignments. Attending Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations as President William Ruto’s guest of honour, Abiy emphasized the longstanding partnership between the two countries, highlighting cooperation in electricity, telecommunications, trade and regional connectivity. Yet beyond the diplomatic celebrations, the visit coincided with growing tensions involving Somalia, whose internal political crisis has begun complicating its relations with both Ethiopia and Kenya. Although Abiy’s visit was officially centered on Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations and bilateral cooperation, it unfolded against a backdrop of growing regional tensions involving Somalia. The visit did not publicly establish a common Ethiopian and Kenyan position on the Somali crisis, but it brought renewed attention to the strategic importance of their partnership as both countries navigate increasingly complicated relations with Mogadishu. The significance of Ethiopia’s relationship with Kenya extends beyond bilateral cooperation. Both countries have invested considerable military and diplomatic resources in Somalia’s stabilization, particularly in efforts to contain Al Shabaab and prevent insecurity from spreading across their borders. However, Somalia’s confrontation between its federal government and regional political actors is creating disagreements over the responsibilities of neighbouring countries. For Ethiopia, the challenge is to maintain its commitment to Somalia’s security without becoming involved in political disputes that could undermine its wider regional interests. The immediate source of tension lies in Somalia’s South West State, where the removal of former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in March 2026 failed to produce a lasting political settlement. Instead, confrontations between his supporters and forces aligned with the federal government have continued, exposing deeper disagreements over regional autonomy and the distribution of political authority. By October 19, forces loyal to Laftagareen reportedly controlled five towns in the Bay region, including Buurhakaba, Qansaxdheere and Dinsoor, complicating Mogadishu’s efforts to consolidate authority. The conflict is particularly consequential because the South West State includes territories where Ethiopian forces have maintained a security presence for years. According to Somali Guardian reporting published on October 19 , Somali federal authorities requested Ethiopian military assistance against forces aligned with Laftagareen, but Ethiopian commanders declined to participate in what they considered an internal political confrontation. Although the reported exchange has not been independently confirmed, it illustrates a fundamental question concerning foreign military involvement in Somalia: whether security assistance intended to confront common threats should extend to supporting the federal government in disputes over domestic political authority. For Ethiopia, the issue has acquired additional importance following the transition from the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia, ATMIS, to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, AUSSOM, which commenced on January 1, 2025. Under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2767 , the successor mission was authorized to support Somali forces against Al Shabaab, protect civilians and facilitate the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali institutions. Its mandate also encompasses security support for political processes, but does not provide unrestricted authority to determine the outcome of internal political disputes. The transition brought renewed attention to the distinction between Ethiopian troops operating under African Union arrangements and those deployed through separate bilateral security understandings. This distinction matters because forces assigned to AUSSOM operate within a defined multinational framework, while deployments outside that structure depend on separate arrangements with Somalia. In its December 2025 communiqué , the African Union Peace and Security Council explicitly acknowledged Ethiopia and Uganda for deploying additional troops under bilateral arrangements. Their presence cannot therefore be understood solely through AUSSOM’s command structure. Ethiopia’s longstanding involvement in Somalia has primarily been driven by the need to prevent Al Shabaab from developing secure operating areas near Ethiopian territory. The group’s ability to exploit instability and threaten communities across borders makes developments in Somalia directly relevant to Ethiopia’s national security. Ethiopian military operations and participation in successive African Union missions have consequently contributed to a broader effort to contain threats before they reach Ethiopian territory. The South West State remains especially important because the Bay and Bakool regions form part of the wider security environment connected to Ethiopia’s eastern frontier. Participation in Somalia’s internal political confrontations, however, would expose Ethiopia to different risks. Military intervention could associate Ethiopian forces with one Somali political faction, weaken relationships with local communities and transform a defined security commitment into an extended responsibility for political outcomes. Even a successful intervention would not necessarily resolve disagreements concerning federal authority and regional political representation. Somalia’s domestic disputes require political settlements that military involvement by neighbouring countries cannot independently deliver. This position should not be confused with opposition to Somalia’s federal government. Addis Ababa and Mogadishu continue to maintain diplomatic relations and share an interest in preventing renewed militant expansion. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s September 29 visit to Addis Ababa , during which he discussed bilateral relations and regional security with Abiy Ahmed, demonstrated the continued importance of diplomatic engagement despite existing disagreements. Those disagreements nevertheless have a deeper history. The January 2024 memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland, which addressed potential Ethiopian maritime access, produced a significant confrontation with Mogadishu over sovereignty and territorial integrity. Somalia regarded the arrangement as an infringement on its sovereignty, while Ethiopia viewed access to the sea as an important strategic and economic objective. The dispute contributed to Somalia’s closer security engagement with Egypt, which already maintained long winded Nile disagreements with Ethiopia. The December 2024 Ankara Declaration , facilitated by Türkiye, helped restore diplomatic engagement by reaffirming mutual respect for sovereignty and acknowledging the possibility of mutually beneficial maritime arrangements under Somalia’s sovereign authority. Nevertheless, restoring diplomatic communication did not eliminate competing regional security calculations. Egypt’s expanding security engagement with Somalia and its prospective contribution to AUSSOM have introduced further sensitivity into discussions about troop deployments. The African Union’s June 2025 negotiations with troop-contributing countries included Ethiopia and Egypt, demonstrating that both countries were considered within the mission’s institutional arrangements. In December 2025, the African Union also acknowledged Egypt’s preparations for deployment while emphasizing the need to prevent security gaps during the transition. Political endorsement, negotiated contributions and actual troop deployments, however, remain distinct stages. For Ethiopia, any substantial expansion of Egyptian forces near areas where Ethiopian troops operate would raise operational questions, particularly given the unresolved Nile dispute. Careful coordination would be essential to prevent competing strategic interests from complicating counterterrorism operations. Kenya faces a related challenge arising from Somalia’s domestic political confrontation. Laftagareen’s presence in Kenya following his removal has generated criticism from Somali officials. On October 19, Somalia’s parliamentary speaker, Abdikadir Mohamed Nur Jama, reportedly accused individuals residing in Kenya of involvement in activities connected to the conflict and questioned the alleged protection they received. The reporting did not establish evidence supporting those allegations, and Kenyan authorities had not publicly responded at the time. Hosting Somali political figures does not independently demonstrate Kenyan government support for their military activities. Nairobi must balance its diplomatic responsibilities and continued cooperation with Mogadishu against its own legal and national security considerations. The consequences of Somali instability for Kenya are also economic. The Lamu Port South Sudan Ethiopia Transport corridor, LAPSSET, represents an important regional infrastructure initiative intended to expand commercial connectivity and diversify access to maritime trade. Its security is connected to conditions in northern and coastal Kenya, where Al Shabaab has demonstrated the ability to threaten personnel and transport infrastructure. On September 19, 2026, suspected militants attacked Kenyan military personnel patrolling part of the corridor in Garissa. No casualties were reported, but the incident illustrated the security demands associated with protecting strategic infrastructure. Although these attacks cannot be directly attributed to the South West State’s political crisis, prolonged instability in Somalia could place additional pressure on counterterrorism operations and create opportunities for militant expansion. For Kenya, preserving security cooperation with Somalia therefore carries implications for domestic security, investment and regional transport connectivity. Ethiopia shares an interest in protecting these connections, which could strengthen economic integration and provide additional commercial routes. Against this background, the partnership between Addis Ababa and Nairobi offers continuity. Cooperation in electricity transmission, telecommunications and transport has created practical interests that extend beyond individual political disagreements. During his October 20 visit , Abiy emphasized Ethiopia’s electricity exports to Kenya, Safaricom’s presence in Ethiopia and growing commercial connections. Their importance becomes greater as Ethiopia confronts renewed tensions with Eritrea, instability in northern Ethiopia and unresolved strategic disagreements with Egypt. The October 2026 escalation in Tigray and tensions with Eritrea demonstrate the competing pressures confronting Addis Ababa. Strong relations with Kenya provide an additional channel for diplomatic consultation without requiring both governments to adopt identical policies toward Somalia. The coming months will test whether the three countries can prevent Somalia’s internal confrontation from developing into a wider regional dispute. Particular attention should be given to the security situation around Baidoa, changes to Ethiopian and Egyptian troop arrangements, and Somalia’s political preparations ahead of the presidential election announced for May 15, 2027 . Diplomatic engagement through Kenya, IGAD or other regional mechanisms could become increasingly relevant if political divisions deepen. Whether mediation initiatives emerge, however, will depend on the willingness of the parties to pursue negotiation. Abiy’s Kenya visit ultimately illustrates the continuing value of dependable regional partnerships during a period of uncertainty. Ethiopia’s national interests require a stable Somalia, effective cooperation against Al Shabaab and security arrangements that do not unnecessarily entangle Ethiopian forces in domestic political rivalries. Its relationship with Kenya offers opportunities to advance those objectives while protecting economic integration and regional connectivity. The challenge for Addis Ababa is to preserve this partnership alongside constructive engagement with Mogadishu, ensuring that Somalia’s political disagreements do not become another source of confrontation across the Horn of Africa. somalia.content: Consistency in Ethiopia’s Approach and the Evolution of Mediation Channels from IGAD – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 Consistency in Ethiopia’s Approach and the Evolution of Mediation Channels from IGAD 0 Comments The path of Ethiopia and Somalia relations since the mid 1980s offers a clear illustration of how conflict management mechanisms in the Horn of Africa have adapted to changing regional conditions. A comparison of the IGAD facilitated process that produced the 1988 agreement with the Turkish brokered Ankara Declaration of December 2024 reveals both the continuity of Ethiopia’s core security interests and the shifting diplomatic environment in which those interests are pursued. The confrontation that shaped the 1980s negotiations originated in the aftermath of the 1977–78 Ogaden War. Somalia continued to assert territorial claims over the Ogaden region of Ethiopia. Mutual destabilization compounded by internal pressures on both regimes produced a protracted period of tension short of renewed full scale interstate war. At the inaugural IGAD summit in Djibouti in January 1986 Ethiopian leader Mengistu Haile Mariam and Somali President Siad Barre established a joint ad hoc ministerial committee to examine the sources of bilateral discord. Although the committee was formally joint Ethiopia’s representatives led at key sessions by Foreign Minister Lt-Col. Goshu Wolde consistently prioritized recognition of existing international boundaries and the cessation of support for anti Ethiopian groups. This agenda setting approach shaped the substance of the talks. Somalia preferred to sequence confidence building measures troop disengagement restoration of diplomatic relations and prisoner exchanges before addressing the boundary question. Three principal ministerial sessions took place in May 1986 August 1986 and April 1987. Progress remained limited because of these differing priorities. A further meeting between the two heads of state on the margins of the March 1988 IGAD summit in Djibouti provided the decisive political impetus. The resulting agreement formalized after talks in Mogadishu on 3 and 4 April 1988 restored diplomatic relations provided for the withdrawal of security forces from the border ended hostile propaganda terminated mutual support for insurgent groups and arranged the exchange of prisoners of war. Both sides agreed to discuss the boundary question at a later date. In practice the accord ended active Somali claims on the Ogaden and secured Ethiopia’s south eastern frontier freeing Ethiopian resources for pressing internal challenges. The 1988 agreement demonstrated that a regional structure could deliver tangible results when the parties shared a pragmatic interest in stabilizing a disputed border and when one party Ethiopia articulated its security requirements with clarity and consistency. No open interstate war between Ethiopia and Somalia occurred after 1988. Somalia’s subsequent state collapse created a different environment. Under Prime Minister Meles Zenawi Ethiopia engaged constructively in efforts to rebuild Somali institutions helping to shape the transitional federal structure that emerged in the absence of a functioning central authority. This engagement responded first to immediate security concerns arising from the political space along Ethiopia’s border. At the same time it reinforced Ethiopia’s standing as a constructive regional actor. When the Islamic Courts Union consolidated control over much of southern Somalia in 2006 and posed a direct security challenge Ethiopia intervened in support of the Transitional Federal Government. Limited deployments earlier that year preceded full scale action in December 2006. That intervention reflected continuity rather than rupture Ethiopia acted to prevent hostile forces from establishing themselves in adjacent ungoverned space. Serious bilateral tension re emerged only in 2024 following the January memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland concerning commercial and naval access to the sea. Somalia denounced the arrangement as a violation of its territorial integrity, recalled its ambassador and explicitly rejected African Union mediation efforts conditioning any engagement on Ethiopia’s retraction of the memorandum. This stance effectively limited the immediate scope for regional bodies including IGAD to facilitate dialogue on a dispute touching core sovereignty claims. The political climate had become more transactional with parties weighing concrete exchanges of interests rather than operating within the denser shared outlooks of earlier periods. The Ankara Declaration of 11–12 December 2024 facilitated by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, produced a de escalation. The leaders reaffirmed respect for each other’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. They acknowledged the potential benefits of Ethiopia’s assured access to and from the sea while affirming that any commercial arrangements would operate under the sovereign authority of the Federal Republic of Somalia. Technical negotiations were scheduled to begin no later than the end of February 2025 and to conclude within four months with Turkish facilitation available as needed. IGAD welcomed the declaration as a constructive step toward regional stability that external facilitation can complement rather than displace regional mechanisms when circumstances require additional diplomatic weight. In the mid 1980s member state cohesion a bipolar international context that channeled regional diplomacy and a shared interest in border stability enabled IGAD to serve as an effective vehicle. Ethiopia acting within that institutional framework advanced outcomes consistent with its security requirements. Three decades later protracted state fragility in Somalia internal challenges across several Horn countries and the proliferation of external actors with diverse interests altered the diplomacy. Regional organizations continue to perform important roles however on certain sovereignty laden disputes their immediate leverage may be constrained. Ethiopia’s posture has remained consistent across these decades safeguarding the south eastern frontier preventing the establishment of hostile actors in adjacent ungoverned spaces and securing reliable access to the sea. The instruments joint committees under a regional umbrella support for transitional governance calibrated military engagement when necessary and pragmatic external facilitation have adapted to changing conditions. In 2024 Turkish mediation filled a temporary institutional vacuum created by the particular constraints facing regional mechanisms on this sovereignty sensitive question. The 1988 accord and the 2024 Ankara Declaration both illustrate that durable progress depends less on the formal identity of the mediator than on the alignment of core interests and the availability of credible channels for dialogue. somalia.content: The Sodere Initiative and Ethiopia’s Role in Somali State-Building – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 The Sodere Initiative and Ethiopia’s Role in Somali State-Building 0 Comments Ethiopia’s initiative at Sodere brought Somalia’s rival factions into a common political process at a time when the country lacked a central authority capable of negotiating on its behalf. Convened in late 1996 under IGAD’s newly established conflict-resolution mandate, the talks culminated on 3 January 1997 in the creation of a 41-member National Salvation Council, with representation allocated to the four major clan families and smaller communities. Although Sodere did not produce a lasting government, it established a broad-based framework for political representation that subsequent reconciliation efforts would revisit The collapse of the Somali state in January 1991 left political authority dispersed among armed factions, while successive international efforts failed to establish a national government capable of consolidating control. The Addis Ababa Agreement of 1993 brought leading factions into a common framework, but agreement on paper did not resolve the struggle for power in Mogadishu; by the time the last United Nations troops withdrew in March 1995, the underlying competition remained intact. Rivalry between Ali Mahdi Mohamed and the Aideed camp, which passed to Hussein Aideed following General Mohamed Farah Aideed’s death in August 1996, continued to obstruct the emergence of a national political authority. The consequences extended beyond the capital. In the border region of Gedo, Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI) established a presence centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometers from Ethiopia, which Addis Ababa regarded as a base for a movement responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linked to other armed groups opposed to its government. Somalia’s fragmentation thus presented Ethiopia with a problem that international mediation alone had not resolved, the absence of a functioning state was not merely prolonging conflict within Somalia but also leaving neighboring territory exposed to armed networks that could operate across the border. This gave Ethiopia a direct security interest in the restoration of Somali political authority. The expansion of regional institutions in 1996 provided an important foundation for a more coordinated response to Somalia’s political fragmentation, creating a framework through which Ethiopia could address its security concerns while contributing to a regional effort to restore Somali political dialogue. Founded in 1986 as the Intergovernmental Authority on Drought and Development, with a mandate centred on drought and desertification, the organization was reconstituted as the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) following the amendment of its founding instrument in Nairobi on 21 March 1996 and its relaunch at the Djibouti summit of 25–26 November. The revised charter incorporated the prevention, management and resolution of inter-state and intra-state conflicts through dialogue, placing peace and security alongside food security and economic cooperation among the organization’s priorities. This change reflected a broader recognition that the conflicts confronting the Horn of Africa required regional mechanisms capable of addressing their political and security dimensions. For Ethiopia, whose border security was directly affected by the absence of effective authority in Somalia, IGAD’s expanded mandate offered a legitimate avenue for supporting reconciliation through regional diplomacy. The framework connected Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns with the wider regional interest in reducing conflict and restoring political order in Somalia, giving its diplomatic engagement an institutional foundation and a shared regional purpose. Although divisions among IGAD members, including the severance of relations with Sudan by Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda during the preceding year, complicated regional cooperation, the organization’s expanded mandate established an important basis for renewed engagement. OAU strengthened this framework in July 1996, when its Yaoundé resolution recognized Meles Zenawi, then outgoing OAU chairman, as holding a special mandate to facilitate peace in Somalia and supported efforts by IGAD member states to reactivate their initiatives. This endorsement connected the emerging regional effort to the OAU’s broader diplomatic role and reinforced the legitimacy of renewed attempts to bring Somali factions into negotiations. Ethiopia subsequently informed the United Nations Security Council that it had convened the Sodere conference in November 1996 in accordance with an IGAD mandate. Operating within this reinforced regional framework, Ethiopian conduct in the second half of 1996 ran along two tracks that differed in instrument yet converged through local partnerships. On the military track, Ethiopia acted against Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI), an Islamist group that had established a presence in the Gedo region centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Addis Ababa regarded AIAI as a direct security threat, holding it responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linking it to other armed networks opposed to the Ethiopian government. Ethiopian forces therefore crossed into Gedo on 9 August 1996 to attack AIAI bases, and fighting continued through December. The fourth major assault on the group, launched on 11 June 1997, captured Luuq and Buulo Haawo and deprived AIAI of its last major bases in the region. This military campaign ran in parallel with a political initiative that sought to harness Somali opposition to AIAI and embed Ethiopia’s border-security objectives within a broader reconciliation process. On the political track, Ethiopia convened Somali leaders at the Sodere resort for roughly six weeks of talks, which ended on 3 January 1997 with a declaration signed by 27 leaders representing 26 factions. The declaration created a National Salvation Council of 41 members and a National Executive Committee of 11 members led by five co-chairmen, with authority to speak for the Council and to prepare a Transitional Central Authority or Provisional Central Government, and it committed the signatories to a National Reconciliation Conference at Bossaso. The Somali National Front, a competitor of AIAI for control of Gedo, was among the signatories. That overlap offered Somali opponents of AIAI an institutional route to national standing and tied a border security objective to a political process that Somali actors could own. The composition of the Council contains the process’s most durable contribution. Nine seats went to each of the four major clan families, Darod, Hawiye, Rahanweyn and Dir, and five to smaller groups, a distribution that totals 41 and approximates the half-share later formalized for minorities under the 4.5 formula. For the first time the Darod accepted parity among the main clan families. That principle of clan-family parity, first given institutional expression at Sodere, was subsequently formalized at the Arta conference in 2000 and then applied at scale by the Mbagathi process, which in 2004 allocated 61 seats to each of the four major families and 31 to the minority bloc within a 275-member Transitional Federal Parliament. By converting a contest over who speaks for Somalia into a bounded negotiation over who sits within each family’s allotment, parity supplied the mechanism through which Sodere moved Somali politics from open military competition toward transitional institutions. Sodere’s significance extended beyond the representational framework it helped establish to the regional diplomacy through which that framework was pursued. Ethiopia’s subsequent involvement in Somali reconciliation formed part of a recurring pattern that included hosting the 1993 Addis Ababa conference, convening Sodere in 1996 and 1997, participating in the IGAD-mediated Mbagathi talks that produced the Transitional Federal Charter in 2004, and contributing troops to the African Union missions in Somalia, AMISOM and ATMIS, and now AUSSOM. The Mbagathi record offers particularly clear evidence that Somali actors themselves regarded Ethiopia’s participation as consequential. In February 2004, six faction leaders of the Somali Restoration and Reconstruction Council announced that they would stay out of the final phase of the talks while Ethiopia was absent from the table. Hussein Aideed, who had succeeded his father General Mohamed Farah Aideed in 1996 and had remained outside the Sodere process the following year, now argued that a regional peace process required consensus among neighbouring states as well as among Somalis. His position marked a shift from contesting Ethiopia’s involvement in 1997 to treating the participation of neighboring states as a condition of a credible settlement, illustrating how the regional approach embodied at Sodere became an established feature of subsequent Somali peace negotiations. This historical experience has direct relevance as Somalia confronts a demanding security transition, with Al-Shabaab continuing to threaten state consolidation, domestic political negotiations remaining unsettled after the inconclusive May 2026 talks, and AUSSOM’s operational future facing growing financial uncertainty following Washington’s announced intention to end its support for UN logistics and operations from 2027. Ethiopia’s renewed commitment to AUSSOM, reaffirmed at the August 2026 troop-contributing countries summit, provides an important basis for strengthening this regional security relationship. Somalia’s current security transition increases the strategic importance of sustained coordination with Ethiopia. Al-Shabaab retains a presence in areas of Gedo and Bakool near the Ethiopian frontier, while Washington’s decision to end funding for UN logistical support to AUSSOM after December 2026 adds pressure to the mission’s operational continuity. These developments connect Somalia’s internal security challenges directly to the management of its western border, where gaps in territorial control can enable armed groups to move, reorganize and exploit weaknesses in coordination between security forces. Ethiopia’s direct exposure to these threats, its existing security involvement in Somalia and its capacity to operate along the shared frontier make bilateral cooperation consequential to how these risks are managed. For Mogadishu, the practical priority is to establish predictable arrangements with Addis Ababa for intelligence exchange, border threat assessment, troop coordination and consultation over operations affecting Somali territory. These mechanisms would help align Ethiopian security activities with federal priorities, improve continuity between bilateral cooperation and AUSSOM, and give Somali authorities greater influence over the regional response to threats within their jurisdiction. As Somalia assumes greater responsibility for its own security amid uncertainty over international support, the quality of its coordination with Ethiopia will directly affect its capacity to manage cross-border threats and sustain security across its western regions. somalia.summary: The Sodere Initiative, launched by Ethiopia in late 1996, aimed to unify Somalia's rival factions during a period of political fragmentation following the collapse of the Somali state in 1991. Convened under the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the talks led to the establishment of a 41-member National Salvation Council, representing major clan families and smaller communities. While the initiative did not create a lasting government, it laid the groundwork for future reconciliation efforts by promoting clan-family parity in political representation. Ethiopia's involvement was driven by security concerns, particularly regarding the Islamist group Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya, which posed threats to its border. The initiative's legacy continues to influence Somalia's ongoing security challenges, particularly in light of Al-Shabaab's presence and the need for coordinated regional security efforts as Somalia transitions towards greater self-governance.

All rights reserved. An interview with Ali Omar, by Callum McFadden for WFi . You are a regular international with Somalia. How proud are you to represent your country, and how does playing on the international stage compare with club football? Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Representing my national team is honestly the best feeling in the world. There are certain things you cannot describe unless you have experienced them yourself. "To be given the opportunity to play against some of the best superstars in the world is incredible. I was saying to the lads the other day that the transition from playing for Dumbarton to representing Somalia is crazy. I go from playing in front of 800 people every week to playing in front of between 40,000 and 70,000 people at international level. "You have to come out of one bubble and go into another. You are living in two different realities. One minute you are flying high, and the next you are back at your club, where things are completely different. You have to learn to adapt and switch between those environments quickly. "For me, being able to represent my country and give everything for my nation is the best feeling in the world. There is nothing quite like it." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement What have been the highlights of your international career so far, and who are the best players you have faced? "I have two main highlights. The first was playing against Algeria. Two hours before the game, there were 70,000 people in the stadium. I could not believe it. The passion from the fans and the build-up were extraordinary. "That night I was playing against Riyad Mahrez. Honestly, it was unbelievable. Every time he touched the ball, you would think God had come down. That is how loud it was. The noise was incredible, and you could immediately see why he has had a world-class career. His touch was immaculate, and he was calm under any pressure. "Another big moment was playing against Ivory Coast a couple of weeks ago. I had to pinch myself as I was facing some of the best players in the world, including players such as Yan Diomande, who has just joined Real Madrid for over £100 million, and other quality players such as Nicolas Pépé and Franck Kessié. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "For someone like me, coming from little Dumbarton and then playing against some of the biggest names in world football, it is a massive experience. I feel incredibly lucky and grateful for the opportunities I have been given. "I always tell people that, if you get the chance to represent your country, whatever country that may be, take it and give everything you have. These opportunities do not come around often." You have made a significant impact since joining Dumbarton, both as a defender and as a leader. The club was going through a difficult period when you arrived, but results have improved. How do you reflect on that progress? "When I first came to the club, we were going through a rough patch. But, as we both know, things can always turn around. I felt it was only a matter of time. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I remember playing against Clyde on a Tuesday night and drawing 0-0. When we got back into the dressing room, I called my family and spoke to the owner. I told them that I guaranteed we were going to go on an amazing run because I could feel something within the group. "We then went on a nine-game unbeaten run. The players had given us something to build on, and we secured our place in the league after the club had gone through administration. "We have also made a good start to this season. We have 12 points and are sitting three points off the play-offs, so you can see the progress we are making. We are not where we want to be yet, but these things take time because we are still a relatively new squad. "Unfortunately, we are currently in the process of changing manager following some difficult circumstances this season, so hopefully we can continue building on what we have started and get Dumbarton where we want to be. That is the goal." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement You have also become a popular figure among the Dumbarton supporters. What does the relationship you have built with the fans and the local community mean to you? "Honestly, the love and appreciation I have for the fans is massive. From the moment I arrived, the club and the people around Dumbarton have made me feel so welcome, and that is something I will never take for granted. "One of the things that means the most to me is seeing the kids who come to watch us. From the warm-up right through to the match itself, they are always cheering my name. For me, that is an incredible feeling. You do not take those moments for granted because you understand what it means to those young supporters to have someone they can look up to. "I always try to make time for the fans after games, and when I see people around the local area, I make sure I speak to them as well. It is important to me because football is about more than what happens on the pitch. The supporters give you so much encouragement, and I want them to know that I appreciate every bit of it. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Dumbarton and the community have become really important to me because of how welcoming everyone has been. When you feel that kind of love and support, you want to give something back. Whether that is through my performances, taking time to speak to the kids, or simply having a conversation with someone in the town, I want people to know how much I value them. "The fans are a massive part of what makes this club special. They are there supporting us, and I want to do everything I can to make them proud." How have you found playing in Scottish football so far? "My first thought when I arrived was that I did not think I was going to last because of the weather! Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Seriously, on a Saturday afternoon, it can be so windy that you try to play a diagonal pass and the ball rolls back towards you. You wonder what is going on. "But the beautiful thing is that you adapt to your environment and become accustomed to it. "What I find fascinating about Scottish football is how few teams there are in each league and how often you play one another. You can face the same team four times in a season, which was something I had never experienced before. "The margins are also so small. You can be two or three wins away from the top of the table, the bottom of the table, or a play-off place. It is crazy how quickly things can change. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "You keep seeing the same faces, and you want to do everything you can to get the results. It is a completely different experience from what I was used to, and that is what makes it so fascinating." You came through the youth system at Stevenage before spending time at Queens Park Rangers. What did you learn from those experiences? "The biggest thing I learned at Stevenage was that you have to be mentally strong. You need resilience because things can change so quickly in football. "From my time as a scholar at Stevenage through to my first year at QPR, I learned the importance of patience and controlling your emotions. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "When you are young, you do not always understand why certain things happen or why things do not go your way. You might play one week and not the next. You gradually learn how to deal with those situations as you mature. "Now, at the age I am, I understand why I had to go through certain experiences at Stevenage and QPR. They helped shape me into the person I am today. "I am still not the person I want to become, but those experiences are helping me develop. Hopefully, over the next two, three, four, or five years, I will continue to grow. "Football comes with ups and downs. What I have learned is to enjoy the good times and learn from the difficult ones, because the downs do not last forever. Everything I have experienced has helped mould me into the person I am today." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement You made a big move to Irish League Champions Larne after playing around 65 games for Torquay United, but injuries interrupted your progress in Northern Ireland. How frustrating was that setback? "I played almost 65 games for Torquay in the National League, which earned me the move to Larne, who were in European football at the time. "Unfortunately, while at Larne, I suffered an MCL injury which set me back, and I was not able to make the impact at the club that I would have liked." Although you would never have wanted to get injured, you have previously said that the experience changed you as a person and an athlete. What did you learn from it? Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "When I speak to people about my injury, I tell them that, although I am not happy it happened, in some ways I am glad it did because it created a different person. "When I got injured, I learned a lot about myself and my body. I learned what I could and could not do, and I learned about rehabilitation, nutrition, and sleep. All those things are essential parts of the recovery process. "I do not want to sound negative, but I feel the injury happened for a reason. If it had never happened, perhaps I would not have the mindset I have today. "It made me realise how important it is to look after my body, fuel it properly, and go to the gym four or five times a week. The injury helped me become the athlete I am today because I understand that I need to be strong in every area to maintain my fitness. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I wanted to learn more about the gym and understand my body better. Thankfully, I have not had any injuries since then, and I am feeling healthy and fit." Finally, Ali, you are 27 and arguably approaching your peak years. How excited are you about the next stage of your career, both at club level and with Somalia? "I have told my friends and family that I feel I could play until I am 40. I look after my body, pay close attention to what I eat and make sure I get to the gym regularly. "My injury taught me that these things are essential for a footballer. I know I am doing well, but I also know I can do better. I have set myself short-, medium-, and long-term targets. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "With Somalia, the goal is to qualify for the Africa Cup of Nations. If we do not manage it this time, I genuinely believe we can achieve it in the future. "You can see the development within the national team. We are bringing in better players, and people who have not previously been called up are showing an interest because of the results we have been achieving. "We have World Cup qualifiers coming up, and one of the things I love about football is that you never know what can happen. Anyone can beat anyone on their day. "Nobody would have predicted that little Somalia would take Ivory Coast to the 90th minute at 0-0. That shows what is possible. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Hopefully, in the near future, we can qualify for the Africa Cup of Nations and potentially the World Cup. "At club level, my ambition is to reach the highest level possible. Whether that is within the SPFL, English football, or another league in Europe, I want to give myself the best possible chance of getting there. "I want to know that I have given everything I possibly can to achieve my goals. If I never reach that level, I want to be able to look back and say I did my very best. If I do get there, I will know I deserve it because I have put in the hard work. "For me, that is the most important thing."

He described the thrill of playing in front of large crowds and facing world-class players like Riyad Mahrez and those from Ivory Coast. Omar reflected on his journey, noting the challenges and growth he experienced at clubs like Stevenage and QPR, as well as the setbacks from injuries during his time at Larne. He emphasized the importance of resilience and adaptability in football, particularly in the unique environment of Scottish football. Omar also cherishes his connection with Dumbarton fans, appreciating their support and aiming to give back to the community. Looking ahead, he is excited about his career's next phase and aims to help Somalia qualify for major tournaments.

somalia.content: Somalia’s Misattribution of Security Failure and the fonts of Federal Overreach – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 Somalia’s Misattribution of Security Failure and the fonts of Federal Overreach 0 Comments The federal government of Somalia under Hassan Sheikh Mohamud faces a legitimacy crisis of its own making in the South West State and its response has followed a predictable pattern with the militarization of an internal political dispute, the securitization of a regional rival and the externalization of blame on to neighbouring states. The sequence of events beginning in March 2026 and culminating in the territorial collapse around Baidoa in October reveals a structural failure within Somalia’s federal system rather than an externally orchestrated conspiracy. The rhetorical turn against Kenya and Ethiopia functions less as an accurate diagnosis of the crisis than as a mechanism of political damage control and the evidence suggests that the core dysfunction is internal to Somalia’s constitutional order rather than located in the behaviour of its neighbours. The origins of the current confrontation are domestic and constitutional. In late March 2026 federal forces entered Baidoa and forcibly removed South West State President Abdiaziz Laftagareen following a dispute over election timing and constitutional revisions. Laftagareen had defied Mogadishu’s electoral plans and organized a snap re election prompting the federal government to deploy military reinforcements from Buur Hakaba into the regional capital. The intervention succeeded tactically with Laftagareen resigned and departed for Nairobi and by June a loyalist Aden Madobe had been installed through a regional parliamentary vote. What Mogadishu did not secure however was the political legitimacy of the replacement administration or the acquiescence of Laftagareen’s constituency. This distinction between tactical success and political consolidation is central to understanding everything that followed because it exposes a structural gap in the federal government’s theory of change that the assumption that control of the capital and the installation of a pliant administration constitute effective governance. That assumption is empirically false in federal systems where regional authority rests on locally embedded legitimacy rather than central appointment. The consequences of that legitimacy deficit became visible in mid October . Forces loyal to the ousted leader rapidly seized several key towns in the Bay region including Buurhakaba, Qansaxdheere, Berdale, Dinsoor and Awdinle. Most of these advances encountered minimal resistance with local officials reportedly fled to African Union bases and Ethiopian troops stationed nearby did not intervene. Baidoa itself is now effectively isolated. The speed of the collapse indicates not that Laftagareen commands a formidable military machine but that the federally installed administration in Baidoa lacks rooted local support. When a regional government can be displaced from most of its territory within days by a force that was until recently in exile, the problem is one of political legitimacy rather than external aggression. The territorial reversals are a symptom of a governance deficit, not a military one and the causal mechanism runs from legitimacy to territorial control rather than in the reverse direction. Mogadishu’s response to this reversal has been to reframe a political setback as a counterterrorism emergency. The National Committee for Combating Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism added Laftagareen, former Custodial Corps commander Mahad Shub and eight others to a financial sanctions list over suspected links to Al Shabaab . The committee stated that the designations were based on assessed evidence of financial support for the militant group but the published decision did not disclose the specific evidence against each individual. This evidentiary opacity is not incidental and it is structurally necessary to the deflection strategy. A sanctions regime that operates without public evidentiary standards allows the government to impose material costs on political rivals while maintaining the rhetorical cover of counterterrorism. The designation functions as a political instrument dressed in security terminology and its effectiveness depends precisely on the absence of the evidentiary transparency that would ordinarily accompany criminal or terrorist designation. The externalization of blame followed immediately. Parliamentary Speaker Abdikadir Jama criticized Ethiopia for allegedly standing by as forces seized towns where Ethiopian troops were deployed and accused Kenya of hosting sanctioned individuals. The speaker demanded that the federal government seek explanations from Ethiopian troops serving under AUSSOM and questioned how Al Shabaab could capture areas where Ethiopian forces were present. These accusations perform a specific political function: they shift the locus of accountability from Mogadishu’s failed intervention to the supposed negligence or complicity of its neighbours. In structural terms, this is a classic externalization move in which domestic institutional failure is recoded as foreign sabotage. The move is analytically distinguishable from a genuine security assessment because it proceeds without a corresponding investigation, without evidentiary disclosure and without any adjustment to the federal governments own operational posture in the affected areas. The reality of the neighbouring states positions is considerably more mundane and does not support the conspiracy narrative. Kenya has historically served as a political space for Somali actors across the spectrum and no bilateral extradition treaty exists between Nairobi and Mogadishu. Kenyan authorities have resisted pressure to hand over Laftagareen but this reflects a policy of hosting Somali political figures rather than a deliberate campaign to destabilize Somalia. kenya’s posture is consistent with its regional role as a venue for Somali political accommodation not with active sponsorship of insurgency. Ethiopian commanders in the Bay and Bakool regions have reportedly declined to join the political war against Laftagareen citing their counterterrorism mandate under AUSSOM. The Ethiopian position is that its troops are deployed to fight Al Shabaab not to adjudicate Somali elite power struggles. This is a defensible reading of a peace enforcement mandate not evidence of hostile intent. Neither neighbour is actively running the insurgency and both are declining to fully subordinate their mandates to political objectives. The distinction between non subordination and hostility is crucial because the federal government’s rhetoric systematically collapses the two. The structural dimensions of the crisis extend beyond South West State. Puntland and Jubaland have both expressed opposition to Mogadishu’s constitutional and electoral reforms and the pattern of central overreach followed by regional resistance is replicating across federal member states. The South West intervention was not an isolated act of strong governance and it was the first major expression of a broader centralizing impulse that treats federalism as an obstacle to be managed rather than a constitutional framework to be negotiated. When the federal government chose military force over political negotiation it signaled that the constitutional division of powers was subordinate to presidential preference. This precedent has implications beyond Bay and Bakool because it establishes a template for center region relations that other federal member states can reasonably expect to face. The replication pattern suggests that the South West episode is not an aberration but a structural feature of the current federal government’s approach to center region relations. The labeling of political rivals as terrorists is a familiar structural move in states where institutional mechanisms for resolving intra government disputes are weak or absent. When the constitutional order provides no effective forum for negotiating power sharing between the center and regions and when electoral processes are manipulated or rejected by the center, the incentives for securitizing political opposition become overwhelming. The federal government’s sanctions list and its parliamentary speaker’s accusations against Kenya and Ethiopia should be read in this light. They are not analytical descriptions of the conflict but they are instruments in it. The securitization of domestic opponents serves three functions simultaneously, it delegitimizes rivals, it justifies coercive measures that would otherwise require judicial process and it creates an external scapegoat for outcomes that are internally generated. Each of these functions is separable from the others and each can be evaluated on its own terms but their combination produces a self reinforcing cycle in which political failure generates securitization, securitization generates external blame and external blame generates further political failure by foreclosing negotiation. The core problem is not Kenyan or Ethiopian machination. It is a federal system in which the center has demonstrated a willingness to use military force against regional leaders has installed replacement administrations with shallow local roots and has then attributed the predictable consequences of those choices to foreign interference. The anti Kenya and anti Ethiopia rhetoric is damage control, an attempt to reframe a self inflicted political crisis as a story of external betrayal. Kenya and Ethiopia are not actively running the insurgency and they are simply refusing to fully subordinate themselves to Mogadishu’s political goals and that refusal is being recoded as hostility. Until Mogadishu confronts the structural deficiencies in its approach to federalism , the absence of genuine negotiation, the reliance on coercion and the legitimacy gap of its installed allies, the pattern will repeat. The towns around Baidoa are not the last to be lost to this logic and the neighbours will continue to serve as convenient explanations for failures that originate closer to home. The federal government's intervention to remove South West State President Abdiaziz Laftagareen led to a lack of local support for the new administration, resulting in rapid territorial losses. The government's response has involved framing these setbacks as counterterrorism efforts, further complicating the political landscape. The article argues that the core issue lies in the federal government's approach to governance and federalism, which relies on coercion rather than negotiation, perpetuating a cycle of failure and external blame.

Anadolu Agency WORLD Published October 21,2026 05:16 PM Subscribe Nearly 874,000 people could be displaced in Somalia over the next three months as heavy rainfall and rising rivers threaten communities already affected by drought and repeated displacement, the UN migration agency warned Wednesday. In a statement, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said projections developed with the Danish Refugee Council estimate that 874,319 people could be displaced between October and December, with flooding accounting for 92% of the total. "We are looking at the possibility of hundreds of thousands of people losing their homes in just a matter of weeks," said Manuel Marques Pereira, IOM Somalia chief of mission. The warning comes as Somalia enters a rainy season forecast to bring above-normal rainfall amid strengthening El Nino conditions. IOM said it has secured only 14.4% of the $16.62 million required to prepare for and respond to flooding, with the funding intended to assist more than 517,000 people. Beletweyne and Gaalkacyo face particularly "greatest threat," with nearly 229,000 and 82,000 people, respectively, at risk of displacement. The agency said rising river levels and heavy rainfall are already threatening communities, while flooding could destroy crops, contaminate water sources and disrupt access to healthcare. IOM urged immediate international funding to strengthen early warning systems, prepare evacuation routes and provide emergency shelter, clean water and sanitation. football.content: نتائج ذهاب دور الـ32 من دوري أبطال أفريقيا | يلاكورة المباريات أخبار دوريات وبطولات مالتيميديا كلام فى الكورة TV 2026 جميع الحقوق محفوظة لدى السويحلي يسقط الترجي وتعادل صنداونز.. نتائج ذهاب دور الـ32 من دوري أبطال أفريقيا مباراة السويحلي مع الترجي كتب: مصطفى جمال الأحد 18 أكتوبر 2026 11:03 م 0 أقيمت اليوم الأحد عدة مواجهات مثيرة، في ذهاب دور الـ32 من بطولة دوري أبطال أفريقيا، جاء على رأسها انتصار السويحلي الليبي على حساب الترجي الرياضي التونسي، وتعادل ماميلودي صنداونز الجنوب إفريقي مع ويلييت الأنجولي. وتفوق السويحلي الليبي على ملعبه بهدف دون رد، على حساب الترجي التونسي، ليشعل المنافسة بين الفريقين على بطاقة الصعود لمرحلة المجموعات، قبل لقاء الإياب في تونس. وخرج ماميلودي صنداونز الجنوب إفريقي بتعادل سلبي أمام ويلييت الأنجولي، ليحافظ على نظافة شباكه خارج ملعبه، بينما انتصر الهلال السوداني على حساب سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بهدفين دون رد، ليضع قدمًا في مرحلة المجموعات. إعلان وفرط المغرب الفاسي في تقدمه أمام أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري، لينتهي اللقاء الذي أقيم في المغرب بالتعادل بنتيجة 1-1، بينما سقط مولودية الجزائر في فخ الهزيمة خارج ملعبه على يد إينوجو رينجرز، بهدفين دون رد. وخسر فريق بترو أتلتيكو الأنجولي بشكل مفاجئ خارج ملعبه، بثنائية نظيفة على يد سكوتلاند الزيمبابوي، وتغلب حوريا كوناكري الغيني على المريخ السوداني بهدف دون رد. وخطف فريق كولومب الكاميروني فوزًا ثمينًا خارج أرضه على ملعب تونجيث السنغالي، بثنائية نظيفة، ليقترب أكثر من الصعود للمرحلة المقبلة وهي دور المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا. دوري أبطال أفريقيا الترجي صنداونز السويحلي بترو أتلتيكو الهلال السوداني مولودية الجزائر المريخ السوداني المغرب الفاسي 0 نجم صنداونز: نستطيع التتويج مجددا بدوري الأبطال.. اللعب أمام جماهيرنا مختلف جولة الحسم.. مواعيد مباريات إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني لدوري أبطال أفريقيا التعليقات دوري أبطال أفريقيا الأخبار ترتيب الفرق نتائج المباريات مالتيميديا شاهد كل المباريات
